place.en: Black Pine Ridge · under the cliff

setup.zh: 谷口的藤墙为她让开了路；她咳出一口银色的血，化成小狐狸伏在你肩上发抖。你爬上石缝；头顶上，爹拿腰带和绑腿接成一根布绳，吊在崖上喊你的名字。
setup.en: The wall of vines parts for her; she coughs silver blood and becomes a small fox trembling on your shoulder. You climb the crack in the rock; above you, Father hangs on a rope of belt and leggings knotted together, calling your name.

recap.zh: 你爬上了崖，爹一把抓住了你——他喊了你一夜，天亮时拿腰带绑腿接成布绳往崖下爬；阿禾的爹老周顺着你的记号寻来，拽住了他。银月咳着银色的血，伏在你肩上，只有你看得见。
recap.en: You climbed back up and Pa caught hold of you — he had called for you all night, and at dawn knotted his belt and leg wrappings into a cloth rope and started down the cliff; Ahe's father, Old Zhou, followed your marks in and held on to him. Yinyue, coughing silver blood, lay on your shoulder, seen by you alone.

zh: 肩上一团银，一直在发抖。
en: The wall of vines opens a way.
A curl of silver on your shoulder, trembling.
From the clifftop, a hand reaches down.

story.zh:
那山谷的出口，是沈小满找着的。

他找得极急。他爹那条左膝，平地上走路都要先拿脚尖试一试，黑松岭这一道崖，他爹要是爬下来，便不用再爬上去了。

这话银月是不认的：本王早知道出口在哪里，只是腿有点软，让凡人先探一探路。

小满想起他爹的话：先看风。他从头上拔下一根头发——这回学乖了，离银月远远的——捏着举在半空，那头发往西一飘，飘得很是坚决。四面是崖的谷里，风只往一处吹，东边便有一个口子。

他顺着风往东跑，跑到后来，两边崖壁只剩一道一人来宽的石缝，缝口上密密层层挂满了藤，藤条比他胳膊还粗。可风是从藤缝里钻进来的，带着一股松针的味道。

他回头道：「出口在这儿。」

银月早已站在他身后了，懒洋洋地把下巴一抬，拿两个鼻孔对着他，道：「本王正要说。」

柴刀昨儿滚下崖的时候丢了。他正急得要拿牙去咬，银月已越过他走上前去，对着那面藤墙，淡淡地说了两个字：「让开。」

只见那藤墙簌簌一抖，藤叶上挂着的雨珠一齐亮了一亮，像有人隔着藤吹了一口气。跟着，便像一群给主人喝住了的狗，一根一根，缩头缩脑地缩了回去。不过眨眼之间，藤墙上已让出一条刚够一个人走的路来。

小满张大了嘴，回头看她。便在这时，他瞧见她身子晃了一晃，伸手捂住了嘴，咳了一声。这一声咳得极轻，她的指缝里却漏将出来几滴东西，落在草上，亮晶晶的，是银色的血。

小满抢上一步要去扶，手还没伸到，她已不见了。只觉肩膀上一沉，一只巴掌大的小银狐已蹲在了那里，尾巴绕过他的脖子，凉凉的，软软的。它嘴也没动，声音却直接落进了他的耳朵里：「看什么。没见过妖王咳血？」顿了一顿，那声音低下去，倒像在跟自己赌气：「本王原先站在九阶上头。本王如今，跌到了金丹。」又道：「跌下来那一回，本王吞了一颗九转还魂丹——就凭那一颗，吊住了本王这口气。」小满道：「那现在呢？」「化一回形，薄一分。醒一回，也薄一分。薄到底了，就只能一直睡下去。」「睡多久？」「本王怎么知道。……走你的路。」

小满僵着脖子，一动也不敢动，问道：「别人看得见你吗？」

「本王只肯让你看见。别人看你，就是一个脖子上缠了条灰不溜秋旧狗皮的傻孩子。」

小满想了一想，说道：「……那我得先谢谢你。」

「谢什么？」

「这是我这辈子，穿过最贵的衣裳。」

它没有说话，可趴在他肩上的那团毛，一直在抖，也不知是笑的，还是冷的，还是疼的。小满没有问。
story.en:
It was Shen Xiaoman who found the way out of the valley.

He looked for it in a great hurry. His father's left knee had to test the ground with its toes even on the flat; if his father climbed down this cliff on Black Pine Ridge, he'd never need to climb up anything again.

Yinyue wouldn't admit this. This queen had known where the way out was all along; her legs were just a little weak, so she was letting the mortal scout ahead.

Xiaoman remembered what his father had said: first read the wind. He plucked a hair from his head — he'd learned his lesson this time, and kept well away from Yinyue — and held it up in the air. The hair floated west, and very decidedly. In a valley walled with cliffs on every side, if the wind blew one way only, then there was a gap on the east.

He ran east with the wind, and in the end the two cliff walls narrowed to a crack in the rock just wide enough for one person, with a thick curtain of vines hanging across its mouth, vines thicker than his arm. But the wind was squeezing in through the gaps in them, bringing a smell of pine needles with it.

He turned round. "The way out's here."

Yinyue was already standing behind him. She lifted her chin lazily, pointed both nostrils at him, and said, "This queen was just about to say so."

His woodcutter's knife had been lost yesterday when he rolled down the cliff. He was desperate enough to try his teeth on the vines when Yinyue stepped past him, faced the wall of vines, and said two words, quite calmly: "Move aside."

The wall of vines gave a rustling shiver. The raindrops hanging on the leaves all brightened at once, as if someone had blown a breath through the vines from the other side. Then, like a pack of dogs called off by their master, they drew back one by one, heads ducked, tails tucked. In the blink of an eye the vine wall had opened a path just wide enough for one person.

Xiaoman's mouth fell open. He turned to look at her. At that moment he saw her sway, put a hand over her mouth and cough. It was the faintest cough, but a few drops of something leaked between her fingers and fell on the grass, glittering. Silver blood.

Xiaoman sprang forward to hold her up, but before his hand reached her she was gone. His shoulder suddenly felt heavier: a little silver fox the size of his palm was crouched there, its tail curled round his neck, cool and soft. Its mouth didn't move, but its voice dropped straight into his ear: "What are you staring at? Never seen a demon queen cough blood?" A pause, and the voice sank lower, as if it were sulking at itself: "This queen used to stand above the ninth rank. This queen has now fallen to Core Formation." Then: "When this queen fell, this queen swallowed a Nine-Turn Soul-Return Pill — that one pill is all that's holding this queen's breath in." Xiaoman said, "And now?" "Every time I take human form, I wear thinner. Every time I wake, I wear thinner too. Worn through, I can only sleep and sleep." "Sleep for how long?" "How should this queen know? …Walk."

Xiaoman held his neck stiff and didn't dare move it an inch. "Can other people see you?"

"This queen lets only you see. To anyone else, you're a silly boy with a scruffy old grey dog pelt round his neck."

Xiaoman thought about it. "…Then I'd better thank you first."

"For what?"

"This is the most expensive thing I've ever worn."

It didn't say anything, but the ball of fur lying on his shoulder kept trembling, and whether it was laughing or cold or hurting, there was no telling. Xiaoman didn't ask.

exits.means: climbs up, takes father's hand, goes back to him

what.zh: 天没亮便顺着你刻的那四十一道记号寻进黑松岭，扛着门板来找你。
what.en: Before dawn he followed the forty-one marks you cut into Black Pine Ridge, carrying a door-plank to bring you home.

story.zh:
出了那道石缝，小满顺着崖根往回绕，找着一道斜斜的石缝，从崖底一直裂到崖腰，缝里长着几丛野荆。崖腰往上，便是昨儿他爹膝盖罢工的那道坡了。

他往上爬。左手腕肿着，使不上力，只得右手抓一根荆条，把身子送上去半尺，松开，再去抓上面一根。松开的那一眨眼，肩上那团毛便把爪子收紧一分。

爬到一半，石缝里有一块凸出来的石头，刚好容得下半个屁股。小满坐上去喘气，对着肩上那团毛，清了清嗓子。她帮他开了藤墙，咳出了血——有些话，是该趁这时候说的。

他郑重其事地道：「银月。」「嗯，你说。」

「我想跟你说——」

「你爹下来了。」小满一愣。

「一根腰带，两条绑腿，接起来不够两丈，」它的声音很低，「他拴在坡上一棵松树根上，已经吊下来半截了。……先应他。」

小满猛一抬头。头顶上一阵土屑簌簌往下掉，两丈来高的地方，崖壁上吊着一个人，两只手攥着一根打了好几个结的布绳，一只脚在崖壁上乱蹬，另一只脚——左脚——直直地垂着，使不上一点劲。那人嘴里还在喊，嗓子哑得几乎听不出是人声，一遍一遍，喊的是他的名字。

他憋足了一口气，扯着嗓子喊了一声：「爹——！」上头那个喊声，登时便断了。

便在这时，坡顶上一阵大乱。先是一个粗嗓门叫道：「——在这儿！绳上有人！底下也有人！」却是阿禾她爹[老周]{注=laozhou}，一个粗手大脚的庄稼汉，脸膛黑红，一开口，半面坡都听得见。那根布绳猛地一紧，往上收了两尺——坡顶上「咔」的一声，那棵松树根断了半截，他爹整个人往下一坠，一尺，两尺。他一声也没喊。上头几只手一齐扑下来，死死攥住了绳头。他爹贴在崖壁上，却不往上走，反倒伸下一只手来。

小满手脚并用，一口气往上爬，左手腕疼得眼前一阵一阵发黑，也顾不得了。

那只手五根指头张着，指甲缝里全是泥，往下伸着，伸得太长了，长得不像一只人的手。小满认得这只手。昨儿在这道坡上，它擦过他的手腕，没抓住。

他伸出右手，抓住了它。

这一回，它抓住了。

上头的人一齐发一声喊，爷儿俩给一寸一寸地拽了上去。小满还没站稳，已给一把搂进了一个怀里，搂得喘不过气来。他爹整个人都在抖，抖得比肩上那只狐狸还厉害。老周趴在坡边上，两只手还死死攥着他爹的裤腰——腰带早解下来当了绳子——正是昨儿小满攥过的那个地方。

他爹就那么搂着儿子，嘴张着，一个字都没喊出来。

小满说道：「爹，我没事。你的膝盖——」

他爹只道：「闭嘴。」

这是小满这辈子，第一次听他爹凶他。

给这一搂，肩上那团毛一声也没出，缠着他脖子的那条尾巴，却一点一点地松开了。

老周他们带了两根麻绳、一副门板，门板是预备抬人用的。他们天没亮便认着小满刻的那四十一道记号寻了进来。老周见小满囫囵个儿地站着，瞧了瞧那副门板，又瞧了瞧他，好像有点替它可惜，道：「得，白扛上来了。」

小满瞧着那副门板，心想：老周，一夜没睡，两根麻绳，一副门板。这一笔，不是鸡蛋，不能拿两个还一个。他还不知道拿什么还，便先记着。
story.en:
Out of the crack in the rock, Xiaoman worked his way back along the foot of the cliff and found a slanting fissure that split the cliff from the bottom to halfway up, with clumps of wild thorn growing in it. Above that halfway point was the slope where his father's knee had walked off the job yesterday.

He climbed. His left wrist was swollen and had no strength in it, so he could only grab a thorn stem with his right hand, push himself up half a foot, let go, and reach for the next one up. Every time he let go, for that one blink, the ball of fur on his shoulder tightened its claws a little.

Halfway up there was a rock jutting out of the fissure, just big enough for half a backside. Xiaoman sat on it to catch his breath and cleared his throat at the ball of fur on his shoulder. She'd opened the vine wall for him and coughed up blood — some things ought to be said at a moment like this.

Very formally, he said, "Yinyue." "Mm. Go on."

"I wanted to tell you—"

"Your father is coming down." Xiaoman stopped short.

"One belt, two leg wrappings, tied together, not even twenty feet," its voice was very low. "He's tied it to a pine root on the slope, and he's already hanging halfway down. …Answer him first."

Xiaoman jerked his head up. Above him a sprinkle of dirt came pattering down. Twenty feet up, a man was hanging against the cliff, both hands clutching a cloth rope tied in several knots. One foot was kicking at the rock; the other — the left — hung straight down, with no strength in it at all. The man was still shouting, his voice so hoarse it hardly sounded human, over and over, and what he was shouting was Xiaoman's name.

He filled his lungs and yelled at the top of his voice: "Pa—!" The shouting above stopped dead.

Just then there was an uproar at the top of the slope. First a big rough voice shouted, "—Here! Someone on the rope! Someone below too!" It was Ahe's father, [Old Zhou]{注=laozhou}, a big-handed, big-footed farmer with a dark red face, who could be heard over half the hillside when he opened his mouth. The cloth rope snapped taut and was pulled up two feet — then at the top of the slope there was a *crack*: the pine root had half broken, and his father dropped, a foot, two feet. He didn't make a sound. Several hands lunged down at once and clamped hold of the end of the rope. His father pressed himself to the cliff face — but instead of going up, he reached one hand down.

Xiaoman climbed with hands and feet, all in one breath, his left wrist hurting so much that things went black in front of his eyes, again and again; he paid it no mind.

That hand, its five fingers spread, mud packed under the nails, was reaching down, reaching so far it hardly looked like a human hand. Xiaoman knew that hand. Yesterday, on this slope, it had brushed his wrist and not caught it.

He reached up his right hand and took hold of it.

This time it held.

The men above gave a shout all together, and father and son were hauled up an inch at a time. Before Xiaoman had his feet under him he was pulled into someone's arms and held so tight he couldn't breathe. His father was shaking all over, shaking worse than the fox on his shoulder. Old Zhou lay flat at the edge of the slope, both hands still clamped on the waist of his father's trousers — the belt had long since been taken off to make the rope — at the very place Xiaoman had grabbed the day before.

His father just held his son like that, his mouth open, and couldn't get a single word out.

Xiaoman said, "Pa, I'm all right. Your knee—"

His father said only, "Shut up."

It was the first time in his life Xiaoman had heard his father be fierce with him.

Squeezed in that hug, the ball of fur on his shoulder didn't make a sound, but the tail wrapped round his neck loosened, little by little.

Old Zhou and the others had brought two hemp ropes and a door — the door was for carrying someone. They'd come in before dawn, following the forty-one marks Xiaoman had cut. Seeing Xiaoman standing there in one piece, Old Zhou looked at the door, then at him, and seemed a little sorry for it. "Well. Lugged that up here for nothing."

Xiaoman looked at the door and thought: Old Zhou, a whole night without sleep, two hemp ropes, one door. This debt wasn't an egg; you couldn't pay it back two for one. He didn't yet know what he'd pay it back with, so for now he wrote it down in his head.
